- The region lives where the person is: inside the full-screen element, else the topmost
  modal dialog, else the body. A region at the end of the body would be inert behind a modal
  dialog and not drawn in full screen. The place is chosen when the message is spoken.
- Sending the same message twice announces it twice.
- Messages sent within about 150 ms are spoken together, in order. Pass a
`key`

for state that
  changes in bursts (a result count, a progress step): a newer message with the same key
  replaces the waiting one. Identical messages in one burst are spoken once.
- On the server it does nothing and renders nothing; the region exists on the client only.

Words are the caller's: pass text built from a message of the component, never a fragment.
Do not use it for ticking text such as a countdown. The returned function never changes.

content.text:
```ts
const announce = useAnnounce()
announce(messages.moved(card.title, column.title))
announce(messages.results(count), { key: "results" })
```

The setter keeps one identity for the component's lifetime, so it can be passed to
memoised children and effect dependencies. It accepts a value or an updater
`(previous) => next`

call reports the next value to
`onChange`

a function passed to the setter is treated as an updater.
A function that waits for
`delay`
milliseconds of quiet before calling
`callback`

with the
arguments of the last call. It keeps one identity for the component's lifetime, always calls
the latest
`callback`
, and drops a waiting call when the component unmounts (call
`flush`
first to keep it). With
`delay`
changing, the waiting call keeps its old schedule.

content.text:
```ts
const search = useDebouncedCallback((text: string) => load(text), 250)
<input onChange={(event) => search(event.target.value)} onBlur={() => search.flush()} />
```

Rules
  - Required columns (pinned, or priority 1) always show, even if that means scrolling.
  - The rest join in priority order (1 → 5, then definition order) while their minimum
    widths fit. The first one that does not fit hides, and so does every column after
    it, so a narrowing container always hides the lowest-priority column first.
  - A user-sized column is fixed at its width: it never grows or shrinks, so a resize
    never moves under the pointer.
  - Flexible columns start at their preferred width, shrink towards their minimum when
    space is short and share spare space (up to their maximum) when it is plentiful.

start when columns are as short as each other. Because every item goes where the columns are
shortest so far, the tops never go back up as the items go on: item *n*'s top is at or below
item *n − 1*'s, and level with it only when it sits further along the row. The order of the
items is therefore the order of reading, which is the order Tab follows, with no

or

is the item's height in px at that column width: from a known
ratio, so nothing moves as pictures load, or a measured or estimated figure. Appending items
never moves the earlier ones; the placement is pure arithmetic, so a host that windows a long
list can run it for all the items and render only those near the viewport.

Items of different heights in columns, laid out from the box's width. Every item goes to the
shortest column so far, so the columns stay level without the content reflowing, and the order
of the items is the order of reading: each item's top is at or below the one before it, and
level only further along the row. Tab follows the DOM, which is that order, so focus never
jumps between columns. (CSS
`columns`

fills a column at a time and breaks exactly this.)

With a ratio for each item, the layout is arithmetic from the width and the ratios, with no
measuring of pictures: nothing moves while they load and the items before an appended one never
move. It renders every item: for a very long list load it in pages, or place the items yourself
with
`layoutMasonry`

and render only those near the viewport. The first render has no width
to lay out from, so on the server the items are present and hidden until the browser measures.

`li`

A typed React 19 component library for glass interfaces, data applications and assistant
experiences. Components use Base UI behaviour, semantic CSS tokens, container queries and
shared keyboard and accessibility conventions.

## Install

Install the versioned package attached to a [GitHub release](https://github.com/Dastari/glass-ux/releases).

React 19 and React DOM 19 are peer dependencies. The tested integration uses Vite 8
and Tailwind 4; the App Router fixture also builds with Next.js 16 and webpack. Supported browsers are current Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari, and
Firefox ESR 140 (the Firefox in Debian 12 and 13). Register
beside the React and Tailwind plugins. Import components through their public entries:

The application owns the Tailwind pipeline, authentication, routing, data adapters and
branding. With Tailwind 4, include the package in source discovery:

holds every component's rules. To load only those of the entries an
application imports, generate a stylesheet with

at
the application root when using their respective components. See the component API for
their props and controlled/uncontrolled state contracts.

Optional server adapters are separate entries. The graphql-orm filter mapping moved from

; see
[Data tables, filters and server adapters](

), with
  [keeping a theme in the project](

), generated from the exported TypeScript types.
- [Typed input guides](

).
- [Live documentation site](https://dastari.github.io/glass-ux/): a studio workspace (charts,
  a grouped project table with drag-to-reorder priorities, sheets and a typed form dialog),
  a scripted assistant chat beside a phone preview, a live network-operations workspace
  (map, site table, device topology windows, review notes and account switching with

) and appearance controls for the six canvas backgrounds, UI scale, corner
  radius and line weight. Copyable page templates cover an overview dashboard, settings, a list
  with a detail pane, an inbox and a file manager. Component family pages combine related examples with section navigation and
  API references for every public export.

Each release also attaches the built documentation site as

, for
hosting the catalogue offline. The package itself carries no gallery or demo code.

All sample organisations, people, identifiers, conversations and values are fictional.
The demo portraits are generated faces approved by the repository owner for redistribution.
They are demo assets; the component runtime never assumes a person or a data source.

## Agent skills

```sh
pnpm exec glass-ux skills install --target agents
```

Six bundled skills cover adoption, component selection, forms, tables and charts, assistant
UI and library authoring. They read the documentation installed with the same release.
The command preserves existing project instructions and requires

before replacing
already installed Glass UX skills.

```sh
pnpm install
pnpm build
pnpm dev             # documentation site on http://127.0.0.1:4220
pnpm dev:flat        # Flat comparison preview on http://127.0.0.1:4230 (also serves the LAN)
pnpm check
pnpm docs:build      # package, API reference and static documentation site
pnpm test:e2e
```

TypeScript 6 is pinned for the TypeDoc compiler API. Consumers may use newer TypeScript
versions. Releases contain ESM JavaScript, declaration files and maps, CSS, bundled fonts,
offline Markdown guides and the generated API model. No build runs when a release package
is installed.
